rows.title: 'Deficits are lower, that's a fact': Finance minister defends budget
rows.summary: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne used a CTV Question Period interview to defend Budget 2026, which was tabled on Nov. 5, arguing that federal deficits are smaller than earlier projected. Last year's deficit came in $27.5 billion below what the spring economic update had forecast, mainly because revenues were much stronger than expected. Even so, the budget shows the deficit rising to more than $62 billion next year and staying above $50 billion through 2030. Champagne said the budget adds about $146 billion in measures, roughly two-thirds aimed at growing the economy and one-third at affordability, housing and homelessness, and he described the spending as investment rather than ordinary expense. Opposition parties attacked the plan from both sides, with the Conservatives focusing on rising debt interest and the NDP saying it does too little to lower living costs.
rows.fact: Interest on federal debt is projected at $60.2 billion next year, more than the $57.4 billion set aside for health-care transfers to the provinces. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called debt interest the fastest-growing item in the budget, while NDP Leader Avi Lewis said it favours corporations and investors over households.
rows.outlook: The cost of interest on government debt is projected to exceed $85 billion by 2030.
rows.why: 정부가 빚을 내서 '투자'하는 것과 그 대가로 늘어나는 이자 비용 사이의 균형, 즉 재정적자의 장단점을 실제 예산 논쟁으로 이해할 수 있습니다.
rows.why_en: It shows the real trade-off of deficit spending: borrowing to invest in growth versus the rising interest bill that crowds out other priorities.
rows.term_def: The interest a government must pay each year on the money it has borrowed. When debt or interest rates rise, more tax money goes to interest instead of schools, hospitals or other programs.
rows.note: Fallback to a 7-day story (Budget 2026, tabled Nov. 5); no major federal policy release in the last 24 hours. Deficit figures cross-checked with CKNX News Today's Nov. 5 budget report ($62.3B deficit for 2026-27; $142.1B in new measures over five years, versus the $146B figure the minister cited).

opinion.title: Lorne Gunter: Carney government budget accelerates growth of Canada's debt-servicing costs
opinion.author: Lorne Gunter
opinion.summary: Columnist Lorne Gunter argues that the budget's smaller-than-expected deficit, about $15 billion lower than last year's projection, comes mostly from luck rather than restraint: oil prices of roughly US$90 to US$100 a barrel for nearly a year are bringing Ottawa more than $1 billion a month in extra tax revenue. He points out that 2026-27 spending of $602 billion is $14 billion higher than planned a year ago, against revenue of just under $540 billion. Citing the Canadian Taxpayers Federation, he notes that borrowing costs of about $60 billion now exceed both GST revenue and health transfers, and that the Parliamentary Budget Officer calls interest the fastest-growing expense. He doubts the government's promise to simplify the tax system and calls the whole fiscal plan fragile.
opinion.why: 유가 상승 같은 '운'으로 늘어난 세수가 재정 건전성을 착시처럼 보이게 할 수 있다는 비판적 시각을 통해, 예산 숫자를 어떻게 따져 읽어야 하는지 배울 수 있습니다.
opinion.why_en: It teaches you to read budget numbers critically, showing how windfall revenue from high oil prices can make public finances look healthier than they really are.

rows.title: Democrats will want to repeal Trump's tariffs. It won't be easy.
rows.summary: After winning majorities in both the House and Senate in the midterm elections, Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, are expected to try to repeal President Trump's tariffs. Martha Gimbel of the Yale Budget Lab estimates the average tariff rate at about 11%, costing a typical household around $1,100, and says tariffs are feeding voters' worries about affordability. Tariffs also bring in a lot of money, almost $2 trillion over ten years by her estimate, so removing them would widen the budget gap. Because Trump is likely to veto any repeal bill, Democrats would need enough Republican votes for a two-thirds, veto-proof majority. Analysts say that is very hard, though a narrower coalition might form around specific targets such as tariffs on Canada.
rows.fact: Democratic majorities in both chambers take over in January, and tariff repeal is expected to be an early target. Yale Budget Lab estimates an average tariff rate near 11%, about $1,100 per household, and close to $2 trillion in revenue over a decade. Overriding a presidential veto requires two-thirds of both chambers.
rows.outlook: Analysts from CSIS and the Cato Institute expect a broad repeal to fail against a veto, with targeted rollbacks, such as on Canadian goods, more realistic.
rows.why: 관세가 결국 누구의 부담이 되는지, 그리고 거부권 같은 정치 제도가 경제정책의 실제 변화를 어떻게 좌우하는지 함께 볼 수 있습니다.
rows.why_en: It explains who actually pays for tariffs and how political rules like the presidential veto decide whether an economic policy can be reversed.
rows.term_def: A tax on imported goods. Importers pay it at the border, but much of the cost is usually passed on to consumers through higher prices.
rows.note: Fallback to a 7-day story; no major new U.S. policy release in the last 24 hours that was not already covered. Published Nov. 5 U.S. time (Nov. 6 KST).

opinion.title: Why Canada shouldn't count on Democrats to repeal Trump's tariffs
opinion.author: Falice Chin
opinion.summary: This analysis walks through the vote math facing the new Democratic Congress: overriding a veto takes 67 senators and 290 House members, so Democrats would need at least 11 Republican senators and dozens of extra House votes. It recalls that the Senate passed three measures against the emergency declarations behind the tariffs in October 2025, but none became law. It adds that the U.S. collected about $173 billion in net customs duties in fiscal 2026, at a time when the federal deficit was nearly $2 trillion and interest costs topped $1 trillion, which makes that revenue hard to give up. University of Calgary trade expert Carlo Dade says the numbers simply are not there, and the author concludes that American protectionism may outlast the Trump presidency.
opinion.why: 재정적자와 관세 수입이 얽혀 있어 정권이 바뀌어도 보호무역이 쉽게 사라지지 않을 수 있다는 점을, 캐나다 같은 무역 상대국의 시각에서 보여 줍니다.
opinion.why_en: It shows, from a trading partner's point of view, why tariffs tied to government revenue and deficits may persist even after political power shifts.

rows.title: S. Korea adds 139,000 jobs in October, above 100,000 for 4th month
rows.summary: South Korea had 29.17 million employed people in October, 139,000 more than a year earlier, marking the fourth straight month of year-on-year gains above 100,000 after employment briefly fell in May. The unemployment rate dropped 0.2 percentage point to 2.0%, and the employment rate for people aged 15 to 64 rose to 70.4%. Young people, however, are being left behind: employment among those aged 15 to 29 fell by 196,000, the 48th consecutive monthly decline, and their employment rate slid 1.7 points to 42.9%. By industry, health care and social welfare added 249,000 jobs, while accommodation and restaurants lost 137,000, the steepest drop since February 2021, and agriculture, construction and manufacturing also shed jobs. The economically inactive population, people neither working nor looking for work, grew by 179,000 to 16.29 million.
rows.fact: Total employment rose 139,000 year on year to 29.17 million, and the unemployment rate fell to 2.0%. Youth employment fell for the 48th straight month, while health and social welfare jobs grew by 249,000 and accommodation and restaurant jobs fell by 137,000.
rows.why: 실업률이 낮아도 청년 고용이 계속 줄 수 있다는 점에서, 하나의 지표만으로 고용 상황을 판단하면 안 되는 이유를 실제 통계로 배울 수 있습니다.
rows.why_en: It shows why a low unemployment rate alone can be misleading, since overall job gains can hide a long slide in youth employment.
rows.term_def: People of working age who are neither employed nor looking for a job, such as students, retirees or those who have given up searching. They are not counted as unemployed, which is why the unemployment rate can fall even when fewer people work.
rows.note: Official data released Nov. 11 (about a day and a half before this edition). Figures match across Yonhap copies in The Korea Herald, The Korea Times, Korea JoongAng Daily and Seoul Economic Daily's own report.

opinion.title: Youth Employment Rate Hits Six-Year Low as Food-Service Jobs Plunge
opinion.author: Hur Sung-soo
opinion.summary: This piece digs into why youth jobs keep shrinking even as total employment grows. It reports the statistics agency's explanations: a base effect from last year's consumer vouchers that boosted restaurant jobs, weak domestic demand, automation such as kiosks and unmanned stores, and companies preferring experienced workers and rolling recruitment, which raises the bar for first-time job seekers. The semiconductor boom is not creating many jobs because chipmaking is capital-intensive. The age split is stark: employment among people in their 20s fell by 203,000, while those 60 and older gained 196,000, and regular employees rose by 287,000 as temporary workers fell by 107,000. A senior statistics official said weak private-sector hiring is partly offsetting government job policies, and the government plans to fund a 2027 Youth Employment Recovery Plan.
opinion.why: 반도체 호황처럼 자본집약적인 성장이 왜 일자리를 많이 만들지 못하는지, 그리고 자동화와 경력직 선호가 청년 취업에 어떤 영향을 주는지 생각해 볼 수 있습니다.
opinion.why_en: It helps you see why capital-intensive growth like the chip boom creates few jobs, and how automation and a preference for experienced hires hit young job seekers.

rows.title: UK economy grows 0.7 per cent as AI boom lifts business investment
rows.summary: The UK economy grew 0.7% between July and September, according to the Office for National Statistics, beating expectations even as energy prices spiked because of the war involving Iran. September alone grew 0.2%, when forecasters had expected no growth. The ONS said the expansion came almost entirely from services, which grew 0.9%, with computer programming growing at its fastest pace in three years as AI-linked businesses expanded; production rose 0.1% and construction shrank 0.7%. The Bank of England has estimated that about a fifth of growth is driven by AI-related investment. Growth has been easing gradually through the year, after 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second.
rows.fact: UK GDP grew 0.7% in the third quarter, with September up 0.2%. Services rose 0.9%, production 0.1%, and construction fell 0.7%, and the ONS credited AI-linked computer programming for much of the strength.
rows.outlook: The Office for Budget Responsibility expects the energy price spike to drag growth down to 1% in 2027, while NIESR forecasts 1.1%.
rows.why: AI 투자 같은 새로운 산업이 한 나라의 GDP 성장에 얼마나 기여하는지, 그리고 에너지 가격 충격이 앞으로 성장에 어떤 부담이 되는지 함께 볼 수 있습니다.
rows.why_en: It shows how a new industry like AI can drive a whole country's GDP growth, and how an energy price shock may weigh on growth ahead.
rows.term_def: The total value of all goods and services a country produces in a period. Quarterly GDP growth tells you how much the economy expanded compared with the previous three months.
rows.note: Sector figures cross-checked with Trustnet's Nov. 12 report on the ONS release (services +0.9%, production +0.1%, construction -0.7%; September +0.2%).

opinion.title: UK economy continues to defy doomsayers but the road ahead is bleak
opinion.author: Joe Nellis (Economic adviser, MHA; Cranfield School of Management)
opinion.summary: Economist Joe Nellis notes that the economy is now 1.9% larger than a year ago and that, unlike in 2022 to 2025 when government spending did much of the work, this year's growth is coming mainly from businesses and consumers, helped by AI-related investment and solid retail sales. He argues that growth for 2026 will beat the OBR's 1.2% forecast unless the fourth quarter shrinks sharply. But he warns that strong activity strengthens the case for more interest rate rises after the Bank of England lifted rates to 4%, with inflation at 3.5% in September and expected by the Bank to reach 5% by mid-2027 because of energy costs. Without a quick end to the Middle East conflict, he expects higher inflation and borrowing costs to squeeze households and businesses so that momentum fades in 2027.
opinion.why: 경제가 강하게 성장하는 것이 오히려 금리 인상 압력이 될 수 있다는 역설을 통해, 성장·물가·금리가 서로 어떻게 연결되는지 이해할 수 있습니다.
opinion.why_en: It explains the paradox that strong growth can push a central bank toward higher interest rates, showing how growth, inflation and rates are linked.

rows.title: Retail inflation hits 24-month high of 6.09% in October, crosses RBI's upper tolerance limit ahead of December MPC meet
rows.summary: India's consumer price inflation rose to 6.09% in October from 5.54% in September, the highest reading since October 2024, according to official data released on Nov. 12. That puts inflation above the 6% upper limit of the Reserve Bank of India's tolerance band, which allows inflation to move between 2% and 6% around a 4% target. Food inflation jumped to 8.94% from 7.74%, led by onions, up more than 116% from a year earlier, as well as garlic, ginger and lemons; rural inflation (6.63%) was higher than urban inflation (5.41%). The RBI has linked the price surge to depleted stored onion stocks and uneven rainfall that delayed the arrival of fresh kharif crops. The central bank already raised its repo rate by a quarter point to 5.50% in October, and its next policy meeting is on Dec. 2 to 4.
rows.fact: Headline CPI inflation was 6.09% in October, up from 5.54%, and above the RBI's 6% upper tolerance limit. Food inflation reached 8.94%, with onion prices up 116.22% year on year. The RBI raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% in October and adopted a stance of calibrated tightening.
rows.why: 식품 가격 같은 공급 측 요인이 물가를 끌어올릴 때 중앙은행이 정한 '물가 목표 범위'가 어떤 의미를 갖고, 왜 금리 인상 압력이 커지는지 이해할 수 있습니다.
rows.why_en: It shows what a central bank's inflation target band means in practice, and why supply-driven food price jumps can still push it toward raising rates.
rows.term_def: A system in which a central bank commits to keeping inflation near a set goal, such as 4%, within an allowed range, such as 2% to 6%. Going above the range signals that the bank may need to act, often by raising interest rates.
rows.note: Headline and food inflation figures cross-checked with Xinhua's Nov. 12 report citing India's Ministry of Statistics (MoSPI). Figures are provisional.

opinion.title: Retail inflation climbs to 2-yr high of 6.09% in Oct, strengthening expectations of December repo rate hike: Economists
opinion.author: Patit Mandal (IANS)
opinion.summary: This wire report gathers economists' reactions to the October inflation data. Radhika Rao, senior economist at DBS Bank, says inflation has not yet peaked because of an unfavourable base effect, expects the RBI to revise its quarterly inflation projections higher, and forecasts a second straight rate hike in December. Tanay Dalal of Axis Bank warns that the figures raise the risk that policy rates may need to go above the estimated neutral rate of about 6%. Anil Gupta, president of the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry, says the food component deserves particular attention. The report also notes that the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee voted unanimously for the October hike.
opinion.why: 전문가들이 물가 지표를 보고 다음 금리 결정을 어떻게 예측하는지, 그리고 '중립금리'라는 개념이 왜 중요한지 배울 수 있습니다.
opinion.why_en: It shows how economists use an inflation report to predict the next rate decision, and why the idea of a neutral interest rate matters.
